overview:
Burundi is a small, hilly country in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, about the size of Maryland, pressed between Rwanda, Tanzania, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its southwestern edge dips into Lake Tanganyika, the second-deepest lake in the world. Burundi is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa: about 13 million people live here, and nearly every hillside is terraced with fields of beans, bananas, cassava, and coffee.

The political capital is Gitega, in the center of the country, while the much larger city of Bujumbura on the lakeshore remains the economic hub. Kirundi is spoken by almost everyone, and French is also official; Swahili is common in trade. Burundi is a republic with a president and parliament. It is one of the poorest countries in the world, and most families live by farming small plots. Yet it is famous for something joyful: its royal drummers, whose thunderous performances, with drums balanced on the players' heads, are known around the globe.
landAndNature: Burundi rises steeply from Lake Tanganyika, at about 770 meters, to a high central plateau and mountains that top 2,600 meters at Mount Heha. Because of the altitude, the climate is mild for a place so close to the equator, with two rainy seasons feeding rivers and the green hills that give the country its nickname, the land of a thousand hills, shared with Rwanda. One of the southernmost sources of the Nile is a spring near Rutovu. Lake Tanganyika holds hundreds of brightly colored cichlid fish found nowhere else, and hippos and crocodiles live along its shores. Kibira National Park, a mountain rainforest, shelters chimpanzees and colobus monkeys, while Rusizi park's marshes attract flamingos and other waterbirds.
peopleAndCulture: Burundians belong mainly to the Hutu and Tutsi groups, with a small Twa community, all sharing the Kirundi language and many customs. Most people are Christian. Daily meals are simple: beans, sweet potatoes, cassava, plantains, and a stiff porridge called ugali, with fish from the lake near the shore. Sharing a jug of banana or sorghum beer through long straws is a sign of friendship. The Royal Drummers of Burundi, recognized by UNESCO, perform with heavy drums carved from tree trunks; dancers leap while the karyenda drum, once a sacred symbol of the king, keeps the rhythm. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Burundian long-distance runners have competed strongly at the Olympics, winning gold in 1996.
history: The Kingdom of Burundi formed by the 1600s under a line of kings called mwami, ruling Hutu farmers, Tutsi cattle herders, and Twa hunters. Germany claimed the area in the 1890s, and after World War I Belgium ruled it together with Rwanda, favoring the Tutsi minority for positions of power and deepening divisions. Burundi became independent on July 1, 1962, at first as a kingdom, then as a republic in 1966. Decades of violence between Hutu and Tutsi followed, including mass killings in 1972 and a civil war from 1993 to 2005 in which about 300,000 people died. A peace agreement brought a power-sharing government. Political tensions rose again after 2015, and many Burundians fled abroad. In 2019 the capital was officially moved from Bujumbura to Gitega.
funFacts: Burundian drummers balance drums weighing dozens of kilograms on their heads while walking, dancing, and playing.
Lake Tanganyika is nearly 1,500 meters deep and holds about one-sixth of the world's fresh surface water.
A pyramid monument near Rutovu marks a spring that Burundians call the southernmost source of the Nile.
Burundi and Rwanda both use the nickname land of a thousand hills.
Vénuste Niyongabo won Burundi's first Olympic gold medal in the 5,000 meters at the 1996 Atlanta Games.
